irascible

ih-RAS-uh-bul · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Irascible is easily prone to anger or outbursts; quick-tempered.

Their landlord flew into a rage if a rent check arrived even a day late -- irascible, as everyone in the building already knew.

Example

The famously irascible violinist once stormed off stage mid-rehearsal because a stagehand's cough interrupted his solo.

Irascible describes someone with a short fuse -- a small annoyance, like a single cough, is enough to trigger a full outburst.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hot-tempered: Hot-tempered means quick to real anger -- shouting, slammed doors, a fuse that burns fast. It is the everyday word for what irascible names more formally, and both describe genuine anger: an irascible or hot-tempered person erupts, rather than merely bristling.

testy: Testy means easily annoyed -- snappish, impatient, quick with a curt reply. It stops well short of anger: a testy person bristles, while an irascible person erupts. Testiness is a bad mood you can wait out; irascibility is a temper people learn to fear.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

even-tempered: calm and steady in mood

serene: calm, peaceful, and untroubled

Where it sits · how quickly the temper flares up — grouchy → irascible → explosive

grouchy vs. irascible: Grouchy is far milder than irascible -- grouchy is everyday crankiness, grumbling about the weather. Irascible means genuinely quick to anger, with real outbursts to match.

explosive vs. irascible: Explosive describes a temper so extreme it can erupt with real force -- an even more intense version of irascible.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — irasc-

root — irasc-: to grow angry (Latin irasci, from ira, 'anger')

suffix — -ible

suffix — -ible: capable of, prone to (Latin -ibilis)

Put it together

Put it together: Irascible comes from Latin irasci ('to grow angry'), itself from ira ('anger') + -ibilis ('capable of') -- literally 'prone to anger.'

Use the root in a new word: ire

Use the root in a new word: ire: His careless remark drew the ire of the entire committee -- the same fiery anger you might recognize from the word irate.

Root Check

Word Choice

Irascible describes a personal short temper -- quickness to anger over small things -- more intense and more personal than quarrelsome (petty bickering) and distinct from bellicose (an aggressive readiness for conflict, often political). It shares its Latin root (ira, 'anger') with irate, a word taught elsewhere in this course.
